author: Pete (comedy_nose)
description:
Project 365 #217: 050822 Jack It In. You probably know that my achilles heel in networking is cabling up RJ45 plugs.

In recent years we've been using Cat6 cable which just seems like an absolute bugger to work with. 

To go with the Cat6 cable we've been using two part plugs. These involve threading the cables through a tiny plastic block and then inserting that into a hollow plug and crimping. They're a faff, and the plugs I make are ugly but they work. I ran out of them today.

I tried using this Cat6 cable with a standard one part plug and just had a nightmare, so I went shopping. 

Screwfix had these feed through plugs and they seem like a good compromise. You cut the ends long, sequence the wires and push them into and then through the plug. This allows you to check the conductor sequence and be confident that every one of the conducting wires is long enough to fully engage with a contact pin.

They seem to work well enough.

author: Anordal
description:
Two ends of a 10 gigabit Cat.6 ethernet cable with different connectors:
Screw connector: M12 X-coded (aka. M12X) is a 12mm hollow metal screw containing a metal tube divided into a cross. The tube and the cross shields one pair of pins in each quadrant. A square peg (visible in the nearest quadrant) ensures correct orientation. The connector type is mechanically stronger than the 8P8C modular connector and doesn't have its latching pin weakness.
Common 8P8C connector: As can be seen, this particular connector is partly of metal, for electrical shielding, but has a latching pin of plastic. As protection for the latching pin, sharkfins on each side of the latching pin protects it from hooking onto the cable and breaking off – a particular weakness of the connector type. Still, the pin has lost its stiffness from regular use and no longer latches. This shows as visible cracks in the plastic at the hinge point.
Brand: Metz Connect
